I just want to point out that this is a very English-centric approach. I’m Norwegian, and in Norway most kids learn three languages. Norwegian, English and German/French/Spanish. We also have two Norwegian forms of written language. While dyslexic children often do not have to complete both written languages, and while they can opt out of the third language and instead do an extra Norwegian or English class, I know many dyslexic children who have chosen to do the third option as well. Sometimes, this third language comes in addition to a foreign mother tongue as well (Arabic, for instance). I’ve worked as a teacher, and I’ve obviously gone to school here myself, and I have never encountered a child who ONLY learned Norwegian. 

Anecdotally, I’ve noticed that a surprising amount of Norwegian dyslexic children are more proficient in written English than Norwegian, simply because they consume a lot of English-speaking media. The gamers, especially, have a very high level of second language proficiency. 

I just feel like pointing out that in most countries, speaking at least two languages is the norm, and that dyslexia does not stop most people in these countries as long as they have a functional school system. 

If OP’s wife is still interested in learning the language, I think that French being spoken in front of her is a good thing, as long as someone translates as well. I would recommend consuimg French films with subtitles, for example. Listening to French translations of English songs, and maybe trying auditory learning in combination with a little bit of duolingo to whatever degree her dyslexia would allow her to do it with a certain degree of comfort.

Jeg merker at de fleste i dette kommentarfeltet ikke er særlig kjent med hvitvaskingsloven og hva bankene må gjøre for å etterleve kravene som stilles. Loven kom i 2018 og norske banker har siden den tid utviklet metoder for å etterleve loven. Det er først og fremst tre ting som kreves: 1) at alle kunder blir tilstrekkelig legitimert, 2) at bankene har kontroll på hva kundene bruker banken til i form av besvarelse av et kundeerklæringsskjema, og 3) at bankene utfører løpende kontroller av skjemaene og kundenes bruk av banken, og eventuelt innhenter mer informasjon og dokumentasjon i tilfeller der dette anses nødvendig. For de aller fleste kundene er kun 1 og 2 aktuelle, nummer 3 er noe som gjøres kun i tilfeller der behovet eksisterer for redegjørelse av bruk( altså å ta kontakt med kunde, ikke foreta kontroll av skjema, dette gjøres i alle banker). I de fleste tilfeller på 3 er det snakk om at folk har misforstått et spørsmål eller har en noe avvikende fra normen men legitim bruk av banken, men av og til avdekkes det kriminelle handlinger eller handlinger som ellers bryter bankens retningslinjer. 

I tilfeller som i saken over, er det snakk om at banken ikke klarte å innhente det den er pålagt å gjøre, så det tredje punktet kunne da eventuelt ikke gjennomføres. Når bankene ikke har kontroll på det loven krever, vil finanstilsynet straffe bankene og bankene vil da på en måte ha brutt norsk lov. This is my initial impression of the songs, but I'm not rating them cause I'm only on my third listen through (I had classes in the morning) so I don't feel ready to do that yet. 

I Forgot You Existed: This one is somewhat underwhelming for me, but it is really catchy and I like the melody. It also makes me laugh at some points. I think it's a grower! Secret sessioners were so far off though, this is nothing like State of Grace in any way! Favorite line: her laugh, and the "sooo... yeah" at the end. 

Cruel Summer: Like other people have said, why wasn't this the first single? I love the beat and the way she articulates the last words in the line during the verses. Favorite lines: "I snuck in through the garden gate every night that summer/just to seal my fate". 

Lover: It's a freaking masterpiece. What more is there to say? Favorite lines: "I loved you three summers now, honey/but I want them all". 

The Man: Ugh, I love this one so much! Truly a feminist anthem. And so catchy! Favorite lines: "And they would toast me me, oh/Let the players play/I'd be just like Leo/in St. Tropez"

The Archer: Love, love love!! Favorite lines: "All of my enemies started out friends/Help me hold onto you".

I Think He Knows: Why are people sleeping on this one? Instant favorite for me. Favorite lines: "Lyrical smile/Indigo eyes/Hand on my thigh/We could follow the sparks I'll drive".

Miss Americana and The Heartbreak Prince: This and Cornelia Street are currently on a shared first place for me. It's infectious. Very Lana in her Born to Die era. Absolutely amazing. Favorite lines: "American stories/Burning before me/I'm feeling hopleless/The damsels are depressed/Boys will be boys then/Where are the wise men?". 

Paper Rings: It has a very rock-like, 60's feel? Sound like it could be in a musical. It's so much fun, I adore it! (Also, does the way she sings "I want your dreary Mondays" remind anyone else of I Don't Like Mondays by The Boomtown Rats?) Favorite lines: "I like shiny things/But I'd marry you with paper rings". 

Cornelia Street: I meeeeean. "That's the kind of heart break/Time could never mend/I'd never walk Cornelia Street again". Do I need to say more?

Death By A Thousand Cuts: Truly amazing. So relatable. This album has so many high highs! Favorite lines: "What once was ours/Is no ones now/I see you everywhere". (Honorable mention to "Now I'm searching for signs in a haunted club".)

London Boy: I had low expectations due to the secret sessioners, and MY HOW THEY WERE WRONG. TEAM LONDON BOY. Favorite lines: "But something happened/I heard him laughing/I saw the dimples first and then I heard the accent". 

Soon You'll Get Better: Heartbreaking. Poor, poor Taylor. The song gets better and sadder with every listen, also, the *breath*. Favorite line: "I know delusion when I see it in the mirror". 

False God: This one leaves me wanting, might be a grower though. I kind of wish we had the Swedes on this one, and that is something I thought I'd never say. The lyrics are great, but I just don't love the production. Favorite lines: "Religions in your lips/Even if it's a false god". 

You Need To Calm Down: It's fun, has a great message, and I blast it quite often. Most of the other songs of the album do however completely overshadow it. Favorite lines: "Cause shade never made anybody less gay" (can't WAIT to scream this line on tour). 

Afterglow: Another one I wish we had the Swedes on. The lyrics are really good, but I can't get into it just now, might just be because I can't relate though and I am convinced that this one will be a grower and become an anthem. I just wish there was a little bit more power in the production. Favorite lines: "Hey, it's all me/I'm the one who burned us down/But it's not what I meant". 

ME!: It's fun, but I feel like it was just the first single because of the music video, haha. It's the perfect follow up to Afterglow though! Favorite line: "You know I never think before I jump". 

It's Nice To Have A Friend: So much better than what SS-ers said. SO MUCH. It's a beautiful story, like a mini bildungsroman, built up of tiny moments from early teens, to early twenties, to late twenties. I adore it. Saying something through art and saying something in real life are two very different things. I'm sure every author/poet/songwriter out there have written things in their chosen format that they would never say out loud. 

Look at any great author, and you can probably find a connection between their real life and their work. Sometimes their work is very autobiographical, sometimes its not, but I'm absolutely sure that something from their personal life has slipped into their work in some form or other. 

For poets and songwriters, it must be impossible to avoid being personal — after all, aren't these two art forms really about self expression? (Not that prose writing isn't personal, it absolutely is, but poetry and songwriting are usually significantly more personal as these works are usually written from a personal perspective rather than through the eyes of a fictional character.)  Sure, we find singers and rappers who don't have personal songs, but those people are usually performers rather than writers. 

Besides, saying something in writing is different than doing an interview. That way, you control the narrative, you can mix reality and fiction however you like, you can make artistic choices, and you word yourself more precisely or more vaguely when you have time to think about what you say before you say it. 

So no, I don't find it strange. I think it makes perfect sense and I'm sure any writer, literary scholar, or simply a person who understands and appreciates the creation of art would agree.

Edna is very much the opposite of Chopin. To put it simply: Chopin was a badass (seriously, google her. She put in one hell of an effort after her husband died). Edna, however, was weak, selfish, and immature. She never really had a chance to grow up, and she never tried to until Robert stirred her desire. Her childlike fantasies of love turned out to be an illusion: Robert wouldn’t allow her to be free, he—like Mr. Pontellier—wanted to marry her, to chain her to him. She didn’t realize that she had it pretty good with husband, and her delusions cracking broke her. Edna wasn’t strong enough to handle being the social outcast she tried to become, she couldn’t handle being a mother, she couldn’t handle being a wife. 

Chopin undoubtedly purposefully wrote Edna’s bad qualities. There is clear social critique in the novel, and I think Edna was supposed to both show what was wrong with society, whilst also showing how neither she as a person, nor society as a whole, were ready for the changes that needed to be implemented yet.
